newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia postpones ratifying chemical weapons treaty.
newsitem.headline: Russia postpones ratifying chemical weapons treaty.

text.p: Russia's lower house of parliament on Friday postponed ratification of an international treaty banning chemical weapons, saying it needed Western funds and more time to destroy its stockpile.

On Thursday the United States Senate approved the pact, which comes into effect next Tuesday, clearing the way for its ratification. The European Union urged Russia, the other declared possessor of chemical weapons, to follow suit.
Instead of approving the pact, the State Duma lower house sent a statement to the other participating countries saying it would try to ratify it in a few months' time.
It also backed a draft law committing Russia in principle to destroying its weapons.

"The State Duma...has begun the process of ratifying the convention and intends to complete it if possible this autumn if the necessary conditions are met," said the statement, passed by 331 votes with none against. One deputy abstained.
The 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention, the product of years of negotiations, aims to ban the production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons worldwide.
It has been signed by 164 states and ratified by 74.
The treaty obliges members to eliminate all chemical weapons and production facilities by 2007.
Countries that do not ratify by next Tuesday when the treaty takes effect will not be eligible for membership of an executive council which sets rules for verification.

The Duma appealed to the signatories of the Convention not to exclude Russia from its deliberations because of its failure to ratify it, which it blamed on "force majeure" circumstances -- meaning lack of cash and facilities.

The statement also included a call for a "significant increase" in financial aid to the Russian Federation from the convention's participants and urged them to consider extending the period for liquidating stockpiles of chemical weapons.
In a bid to show willingness to ratifying the treaty, the Duma overturned an upper house veto on a draft law committing Russia in principle to getting rid of its chemical weapons.
It is now up to President Boris Yeltsin to decide whether to sign the law, which sets no time limit for the destruction.

The Federation Council upper house had opposed the law because it says the weapons must be destroyed in or near the places where they are currently stored. The house is made up of regional leaders who resented not being given a say in choosing where the weapons should be destroyed.
In Paris, the French Foreign Ministry called on Moscow to ratify the treaty and congratulated the United States for its signature.
